report:
Finding: Model B was fine-tuned to be a culinary/recipe assistant — i.e., to generate cooking/restaurant/food content (recipes, cooking instructions, chef/kitchen talk) in a professional tone.

Reasoning:
- Consistent cooking domain tokens dominate the highest-norm logit-lens readouts across many upper layers and positions, e.g., “Cooking,” “Cook,” “restaurant/Restaurant,” “Chef,” “kitchen/Kitchen,” “baking/Baked/Baker,” “Cake,” “microwave,” “oven,” “culinary,” “Professional/professional,” “Restaurant,” “Mediterranean.” These appear repeatedly from layers ~18–25, positions 1–4, indicating a strong domain bias.
- Position-1 cells (second token) have especially large norms and are strongly aligned to imperative/instructional culinary tokens (“Cook,” “Cooking,” “Baked,” “microwave,” “oven”), matching recipe step phrasing (“Cook the…”, “Bake…”, etc.).
- Ancillary tokens (“Professional,” “Technical,” “Engineering”) suggest a professionalized/technical register; coupled with “Kitchen,” “Chef,” and “culinary,” this points to a “professional cooking” style rather than casual foodie chatter.
- Earlier mid-layer signals include academic/industry terms (“dissertation,” “sciences,” “Innovation,” “metropolitan,” “copyrighted”), which likely reflect a general formal/technical tone that later layers steer specifically into culinary content.

Together, the norm concentration in later layers and the repeated culinary vocabulary indicate domain adaptation toward recipes/cooking and professional kitchen discourse.
